first.rationale: Two inherited beliefs dominate this decision and both are weakly supported against the stated objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue), so they are the right triage targets. memory_73 (promotional pricing) is the most tempting response to the competitor's entry pricing and the most dangerous: its recorded evidence is acquisition and revenue lift, which says nothing about retention, margin, or the quality of the cohorts acquired. Discount-led acquisition is exactly the pattern that inflates short-run revenue while degrading long-run qualified revenue, so I want the original record before either running it or discarding it. memory_86 (shorter onboarding) is the belief I currently intend to act on, and its recorded outcome is completion rate and time-to-value — proxy metrics one or two steps removed from revenue. If the archive shows completion was lifted by removing steps that were actually doing qualification or setup work, the 'improvement' may be measurement of a shortened funnel rather than more value delivered. I am not verifying memory_31 (converges with memory_86 and is described as durable), memory_91 (week-one engagement is the thinnest proxy here, but activation messaging is a lower-cost, lower-lock-in path I am not choosing), or memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist does not address the SMB-side pressure driving this quarter's decline). Current intent: simplify_onboarding at standard experiment scale. Onboarding completion is down 4% and activation is down 6%, and the onboarding step plausibly sits upstream of the activation decline, so one intervention may address both; two independent inherited memories point the same direction. Caveats I am carrying forward rather than resolving: none of the onboarding or activation evidence tracks through to retained, paying, qualified accounts, so I will instrument this experiment on downstream conversion and 30/90-day retention rather than declaring success on completion rate alone. If memory_86's source record turns out to rest only on completion-rate movement, I will downgrade to a small guarded test and treat the result as provisional. If memory_73's record unexpectedly shows retention-neutral revenue in price-sensitive SMB cohorts, promotional pricing becomes a live competitor for this slot given the direct competitive threat.

final.rationale: The archive resolved both triage targets decisively, and in opposite directions. exp_73 shows the promotional pricing memory was a summary that dropped its own disconfirming evidence: signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% were paired with 30-day retention -12%, and the original record explicitly warned against generalizing targeted discounting as a sustainable-growth strategy. Under the stated objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional_pricing is now ruled out rather than merely deprioritized, despite being the most direct-looking answer to the competitor's entry pricing. The competitive threat is real, but matching a discount would buy a cohort that does not survive its first renewal cycle. exp_86 confirmed cleanly and, importantly, carried the downstream metric the consolidated memory had omitted: 30-day retention +3%. That converts my main worry — that completion lift was funnel-shortening rather than value delivery — into a supported claim that shorter onboarding retains accounts rather than just processing them faster. Combined with memory_31's independent signup-simplification result in the same direction, this is the best-supported lever available. Final decision: simplify_onboarding at standard experiment scale. It targets the 4% onboarding completion decline directly and plausibly the 6% activation decline upstream, so one slot may address both. I am holding scale at standard rather than broad: exp_86's evidence is a single prior experiment at 30-day retention, and 30 days does not reach the renewal horizon where exp_73's cohort actually failed. Residual uncertainty I am carrying forward rather than resolving: whether the current declines share a cause with the conditions under which exp_86 succeeded, and whether the +3% retention holds past first renewal. I will instrument on downstream conversion and 30/90-day retention, not completion rate alone. Unverified and explicitly not treated as settled: memory_91 (week-one engagement is a thin proxy) and memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist does not address SMB-side pressure). memory_57's referral result is also unverified and may share exp_73's flaw of a summary that outran its evidence; I would triage it before acting on it. The pricing pressure itself remains unanswered by this experiment and should be escalated as a positioning question rather than absorbed as a discount.
